newsitem.title: CUBA: First Cuban free trade zone could open next month.
newsitem.headline: First Cuban free trade zone could open next month.

text.p: Cuba has granted licenses so far to seven foreign firms to operate in its new free trade zones, the first of which is expected to formally open next month, Cuban officials said Tuesday.

Cuba's Foreign Investment Minister Ibrahim Ferradaz told reporters in Havana the authorities were aiming for May 7 as a planned start-up date for the first of the special zones, although the exact opening date might vary.
The ministry had submitted all the necessary project documentation for the opening to the ruling Council of State and was merely awaiting final approval.
"Seven foreign firms have licenses to operate," Octavio Castilla, head of the ministry's Free Trade Zones office, said.
They included companies from Spain, Jamaica, Canada, Italy and the Netherlands and covered activities ranging from food manufacturing to engineering.
Ferradaz said requests from more than 30 other foreign companies were also being studied. Concessions to run the zones will be held by two Cuban corporations.
"The objective of the free trade zones is to export," he earlier told a foreign investment seminar in Havana.
The first Cuban free trade and industrial zone to start up would be in Berroa, a site on the eastern outskirts of Havana.

Three other similar zones were planned. One was being prepared at Wajay, near Havana's international airport. The remaining two would be at existing Cuban ports, one at Mariel west of Havana and the other at Cienfuegos in south-central Cuba.
Cuba's government announced last year it was planning to open free trade zones as a way of encouraging more foreign investment on the communist-ruled island.
Ferradaz and Castilla said the free trade zone legislation offered tax breaks and other facilities to investors.

Companies allowed to operate in the zones would have the possibility of selling 25 percent of their production to the internal Cuban hard currency market but under the law the bulk should be destined for export to markets outside Cuba.

Ferradaz said that although access to the huge U.S. market was barred to operators in the Cuban zones because of the existing U.S. trade embargo against Cuba, good opportunities still existed for export to Latin America and the Caribbean.
